introduction: This intermediate tier transitions to the kinetic mechanics of Nucleophilic Substitution ($S_N1$ and $S_N2$). It details stereochemical outcomes (Inversion vs. Racemization) and maps out the competing $\beta$-Elimination reactions.

core_concepts.title: $S_N2$ Mechanism (Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution)
core_concepts.description:
1. Kinetics: Rate depends on BOTH alkyl halide and nucleophile (2nd order). Rate = $k[R-X][Nu^-]$.
2. Mechanism: A concerted, single-step process. The nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon from the BACKSIDE (opposite the leaving group). 
3. Stereochemistry: Leads to complete **Inversion of Configuration** (Walden Inversion), like an umbrella turning inside out in the wind.
4. Reactivity Order: Strictly governed by Steric Hindrance. $1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$. Methyl halides are the fastest. $3^\circ$ halides almost never undergo $S_N2$.

core_concepts.title: $S_N1$ Mechanism (Unimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution)
core_concepts.description:
1. Kinetics: Rate depends ONLY on the alkyl halide (1st order). Rate = $k[R-X]$.
2. Mechanism: A two-step process. Step 1 (Slow/RDS): The C-X bond breaks heterolytically to form a planar Carbocation intermediate. Step 2 (Fast): Nucleophile attacks the carbocation.
3. Stereochemistry: The nucleophile can attack the planar carbocation from either face, leading to **Racemization** (mixture of retention and inversion, slightly favoring inversion due to ion-pair shielding).
4. Reactivity Order: Strictly governed by Carbocation Stability (+I and hyperconjugation). $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$. Benzyl and Allyl halides show very high $S_N1$ reactivity due to resonance stabilization of their carbocations.

core_concepts.title: Elimination Reactions (Dehydrohalogenation)
core_concepts.description:
When an alkyl halide is heated with ALCOHOLIC KOH, a hydrogen atom is removed from the $\beta$-carbon and a halogen from the $\alpha$-carbon, forming an alkene. 
Saytzeff (Zaitsev) Rule: In asymmetrical alkyl halides, if multiple $\beta$-hydrogens are available, the major product is the highly substituted alkene (the one with more alkyl groups attached to the double bond, making it thermodynamically more stable via hyperconjugation).

core_concepts.title: Nucleophilic Substitution in Haloarenes
core_concepts.description:
Haloarenes are EXTREMELY LESS reactive towards nucleophilic substitution compared to haloalkanes due to:
1. Resonance Effect: The lone pairs on the halogen delocalize into the benzene ring, giving the C-X bond a **partial double bond character**, making it extremely hard to break.
2. Hybridization: The carbon is $sp^2$ hybridized (more electronegative, holds the electron pair tighter) compared to $sp^3$ in haloalkanes.
3. Instability of Phenyl Cation: Rules out $S_N1$ mechanism.
Reaction requires extreme conditions (Dow's Process: $NaOH$ at $623 \text{ K}$, $300 \text{ atm}$ to convert chlorobenzene to phenol).

important_entities.name: Ambident Nucleophiles
important_entities.key_fact: Nucleophiles possessing two different nucleophilic centers.
important_entities.significance:
Examples: Cyanide ($CN^-$) and Nitrite ($NO_2^-$). 
- $KCN$ (ionic) reacts with $R-X$ to form Alkyl Cyanides ($R-CN$, major product) because the C-C bond is stronger than the C-N bond. 
- $AgCN$ (covalent) reacts with $R-X$ to form Alkyl Isocyanides ($R-NC$, major product) because only the Nitrogen lone pair is available for attack.
Similarly, $KNO_2$ yields Alkyl Nitrites ($R-O-N=O$), while $AgNO_2$ yields Nitroalkanes ($R-NO_2$).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Because $S_N1$ proceeds via a CARBOCATION intermediate, it is highly susceptible to **Rearrangements** (Hydride shift, Methyl shift, or Ring Expansion). If a secondary carbocation can shift a methyl group to become a tertiary carbocation, it WILL do so before the nucleophile attacks. Therefore, the major product might have the nucleophile attached to a completely different carbon than where the halogen originally was.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: $S_N2$ is Backside Bulk; $S_N1$ is Stable Carbocation
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To rapidly predict the mechanism: Look at the carbon attached to the halogen. If it's crowded (tertiary), $S_N2$ is blocked (Backside Bulk), so it must go $S_N1$. If it's a primary carbon, carbocations are unstable, so it must go $S_N2$.

exam_strategy_tips: To increase the reactivity of Haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution, attach Electron Withdrawing Groups (EWGs) like $-NO_2$ at the Ortho and Para positions. This stabilizes the intermediate carbanion (Meisenheimer complex) via resonance. A nitro group at the Meta position has practically no effect on reactivity.
